C.	 Market risk
(i)	 Foreign currency risk
	
Foreign currency risk is the risk that the fair value or future cash flows of an exposure will fluctuate because of 
changes in foreign exchange rates. The Group’s exposure to the risk of changes in foreign exchange rates relates 
primarily to the Group's operating activities (revenue and expenses).
	
This foreign currency risk is hedged by using foreign currency forward contracts. The Group manages its foreign 
currency risk by designating forward contracts as hedging instruments against:
	
In case of foreign currency sales and pool of trade receivables in foreign currency-
•	 Highly probable forecasted sales in foreign currency i.e. towards future sales where corresponding exposure is 
yet to be recorded in the books (for an initial part of the tenure of the contract),
•	 Pool of trade receivables in foreign currency (for balance part of the tenure of contract), and
	
Further, the Group settles these forward contracts with banks by utilising it against the realisations for pool of trade 
receivables in foreign currency.
	
In case of imports and corresponding trade payables-
•	 Firm commitments and settlement of certain foreign currency trade payables.

(c)	 Hedge accounting
	
(i)	
Cash Flow Hedge
	
	
The Group uses foreign currency forward contracts to hedge its risks associated with foreign currency 
fluctuations relating to highly probable forecast transactions (forecasted sales). The use of foreign currency 
forward contracts is governed by the Group's strategy approved by the Board of Directors, which provide 
principles on the use of such forward contracts consistent with the Group’s risk management policy and 
procedures. Mark-to-Market Gain/(Loss) on Forward Contracts which are assessed as effective under Cash 
Flow hedge are recognized through Other Comprehensive Income and ineffective hedges are transferred to 
Statement of Profit and Loss account.
	
(ii)	 Fair Value Hedge
	
	
The Group uses foreign currency forward contracts to hedge its risks associated with foreign currency 
fluctuations relating to firm commitments, highly probable forecast transactions to purchase raw materials 
and foreign currency required at the settlement date of certain payables for these purchases and at the 
settlement date of pool of trade receivables in foreign currency. Hedging the forecast purchases and pool of 
foreign currency trade receivables is in accordance with the risk management strategy outlined by the Board of 
Directors. Mark-to-Market Gain/(Loss) on Forward Contracts under Fair Value hedged are recognized through 
statement of Profit and Loss account.
	
	
There is an economic relationship between the hedged items and the hedging instruments as the terms of the 
foreign exchange and forward contracts match the terms of the expected highly probable forecast transactions 
(i.e., notional amount and expected payment date).
	
	
The Group has established a hedge ratio of 1:1 for the hedging relationships as the underlying risk of the foreign 
exchange and forward contracts are identical to the hedged risk components. To test the hedge effectiveness, 
the Group uses the hypothetical derivative method and compares the changes in the fair value of the hedging 
instruments against the changes in fair value of the hedged items attributable to the hedged risks.
	
	
The hedge ineffectiveness can arise from:
	
i)	
Differences in the timing of the cash flows of the hedged items and the hedging instruments
	
ii)	
The counterparties’ credit risk differently impacting the fair value movements of the hedging instruments and 
hedged items

(a)	 Risk Management
	
The Group's objectives when managing capital is to safeguard continuity, maintain a strong credit rating and healthy 
capital ratios in order to support its business and provide adequate return to shareholders through continuing 
growth. The Group’s overall strategy remains unchanged from previous year.
	
The Group sets the amount of capital required on the basis of annual business and long-term operating plans which 
include capital and other strategic investments.
	
The funding requirements are met through a mixture of equity, internal fund generation and other long term borrowings. 
The Group's policy is to use short-term and long-term borrowings to meet anticipated funding requirements.
	
The Group monitors capital on the basis of the net debt to equity ratio. The Group is not subject to any externally 
imposed capital requirements.

on the stock exchange was completed on August 23, 2024.

crore and the premium on buy-back, its related expenses 
and tax on buy-back of ₹277.16 crores, ₹ 2.55 crores and 
₹ 64.57 crores respectively have been adjusted against 
retained earnings.

Note 39 : Significant Accounting 
Judgements, Estimates and Assumptions:
The preparation of financial statements requires the use 
of accounting estimates which, by definition, will seldom 
equal the actual results. Management also needs to 
exercise judgement in applying the group’s accounting 
policies. This note provides an overview of the areas that 
involved a higher degree of judgement or complexity, and 
of items which are more likely to be materially adjusted due 
to estimates and assumptions turning out to be different 
than those originally assessed. Detailed information about 
each of these estimates and judgements is included 
in relevant notes together with information about the 
basis of calculation for each affected line item in the 
financial statements.
Critical Estimates and Judgements
a)	
Current Tax Expense and Deferred Tax
	
The calculation of the Group’s tax charge necessarily 
involves a degree of estimation and judgement 
in respect of certain items whose tax treatment 
cannot be finally determined until resolution has 
been reached with the relevant tax authority or, as 
appropriate, through a formal legal process. The final 
resolution of some of these items may give rise to 
material profits/losses and/or cash flows. Significant 
judgments are involved in determining the provision 
for income taxes, including amount expected to be 
paid/recovered for uncertain tax positions. Further 
a subsidiary Company has claimed deduction under 
section 80IA of the Income Tax Act, 1961 which 
involves significant estimates and judgements in 
respect of sales price of power and steam, purchase 
of goods and services from vendors (Refer note 24).
	
Recognition of Deferred Tax Assets / Liabilities
	
The recognition of deferred tax assets in respect of 
mat credit entitlement is expected to be utilised after 
the tax holiday period of ten years. There is significant 
management judgement involved in determination of 
forecast of future taxable profits beyond the ten years 
tax holiday (which also involves key assumptions like 
future growth rate, profit margins etc.) against which 
the aforesaid MAT credit entitlement is expected to 
be utilised. Any changes to these assumptions could 
significantly affect the recoverability of deferred tax 
asset on account of MAT credit entitlement. (Refer 
notes 6 and 12).
	
Uncertain Tax Position and Tax Related 
Contingency
	
The Group has taken certain tax positions particularly 
those relating to deductions / allowance under Section 
80 IA and Section 36(1)(iii) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 
by the Group. The taxation authorities may challenge 
these tax deductions and accordingly these matters 
are / might be subject to legal proceedings in the 
ordinary course of business. The outcome of the legal

b)	
Contingent Liabilities.
	
The Group exercises judgement in measuring the 
exposures to contingent liabilities which is related 
to pending litigation or other outstanding claims. 
Judgement is necessary in assessing the likelihood 
that a pending claim will succeed, or a liability will arise, 
and to quantify the possible range of the financial 
settlement. Because of the inherent uncertainty in 
this evaluation process, actual liability, if any may be 
different from the originally estimated as contingent 
liability. (Refer note 34).
c)	
Provision / Liability
	
A provision / liability is a present obligation of the entity 
arising from past events, the settlement of which is 
expected to result in an outflow from the entity of 
resources embodying economic benefits that can be 
reasonably estimated. Estimation involves judgements 
based on the latest available, reliable information. An 
estimate may need revision if changes occur in the 
circumstances on which the estimate was based or 
as a result of new information or more experience. 
The Group actualises the provision / liability when 
the invoices are received and the resultant income 
/ expense are recognised in the statement of profit 
and loss. The Group also periodically reviews the 
provision / liability which are no longer required and 
the same are reversed and recognised as an income in 
the statement of profit and loss. Refer note 10 and 11.
d)	
Useful Life Of Property, Plant And Equipment 
and Intangible Assets
	
Property, Plant and Equipment represent a significant 
proportion of the asset base of the Group. The charge 
in respect of periodic depreciation (for property, plant 
and equipment and intangible assets) is derived after 
determining an estimate of an asset’s expected useful 
life and the expected residual value at the end of its 
life. The useful lives and residual values of Group's 
assets are determined by management at the time the 
asset is acquired and reviewed periodically, including 
at each financial year end. The lives are based on 
historical experience with similar assets as well as 
anticipation of future events, which may impact their 
life, such as changes in technology. For the relative 
size of the Group’s property, plant and equipment and 
intangible assets (Refer notes 3 and 4).
e)	
Provision for Inventories
	
The Group writes down inventories to net recognised 
value based on an estimate of the realisability of 
inventories. Write downs on inventories are recorded 
where events or changes in circumstances indicate 
that the balances may not recognise. The identification 
of write-downs requires the use of estimates of net 
selling prices, age and condition / quality of the down-
graded inventories. Where the expectation is different 
from the original estimate, such difference will impact 
the carrying value of inventories and write-downs of 
inventories in the periods in which such estimate has 
been changed. Refer note 8 for details of inventories 
and provisions.
f)	
Defined Benefit Obligation
	
The present value of the defined benefit obligations 
depends on a number of factors that are determined 
on an actuarial basis using a number of assumptions. 
The assumptions used in determining the net cost 
(income) for post employments plans include the 
discount rate. Any changes in these assumptions will 
impact the carrying amount of such obligations.
	
The Group determines the appropriate discount 
rate at the end of each year. This is the interest rate 
that should be used to determine the present value 
of estimated future cash outflows expected to be 
required to settle the defined benefit obligations. In 
determining the appropriate discount rate, the Group 
considers the interest rates of government bonds of 
maturity approximating the terms of the related plan 
liability. Refer note 19 for the details of the assumptions 
used in estimating the defined benefit obligation.
g)	
Government Grants
	
The group has accrued income for Government grant 
related to PPE, in the ratio of related expenses, based 
on eligibility amount. Critical judgement is involved 
in determining whether the Group has fulfilled 
the conditions related to the grant. Estimates are 
involved in calculation of grant income where the 
Group is complying with all the terms and conditions 
of the grant and an application has been made to the 
government and the eligibility certificate / approval 
of grant is awaited. Further, key assumptions used in 
calculation of government grant to be recognized as 
revenue, receivables and deferred income include, 
the future sales growth rate, mix of inter and intra 
state purchases and corresponding input tax credit, 
utilisation of input tax credit, indirect tax rates on 
the products, period of eligibility etc. Changes in 
the assumptions selected by the management 
could significantly affect the recognition of revenue, 
receivables and deferred income related to such 
government grants. Refer note 15.
h)	
Fair value of Financial Instruments
	
The fair value of financial instruments that are not 
traded in an active market is determined using valuation 
techniques. The Management uses its judgement to 
select a variety of methods and make assumptions 
that are mainly based on market conditions existing at

i)	
Ind AS 115 – Revenue from Contracts with 
Customers
	
Ind AS 115 applies, with limited exceptions, to all 
revenue arising from contracts with its customers. 
Ind AS 115 establishes a five-step model to account 
for revenue arising from contracts with customers and 
requires that revenue be recognized at an amount that 
reflects the consideration to which an entity expects 
to be entitled in exchange for transferring goods or 
services to a customer.
	
Ind AS 115 requires entities to exercise judgement, 
taking into consideration all of the relevant facts and 
circumstances when applying each step of the model 
to contracts with their customers. The standard also 
specifies the accounting for the incremental costs of 
obtaining a contract and the costs directly related to 
fulfilling a contract. In addition, the standard requires 
extensive disclosures.
j)	
Determination of Control / Significant 
Influence
	
Significant management judgement is involved in 
determining whether the Group has control/ significant 
influence over another entity in which investment has 
been made by the Group. The judgement affects the 
determination of whether an entity is a subsidiary 
/ associate and consequently required to be 
consolidated in the consolidated financial statements 
of the Group or not consolidated and required to be 
carried at fair value through profit or loss account / 
other comprehensive income / amortised cost. Refer 
note 5 (a).
k)	
Impairment of Non-Financial Assets
	
The Group determines Cash Generating Units (CGU) 
based on management judgement after considering 
cash inflows generated from business activities of 
assets / group of assets for annual impairment testing 
as required by Ind AS 36. Impairment exists when the 
carrying value of an asset or cash generating unit 
exceeds its recoverable amount, which is the higher of 
its fair value less costs of disposal and its value in use. 
The fair value less costs of disposal calculation is based 
on available data from binding sales transactions, 
conducted at arm’s length, for similar assets or 
observable market prices less incremental costs for 
disposing of the asset. The value in use calculation is 
based on a DCF model. The cash flows are derived 
from the budget for the determined period and do 
not include restructuring activities that the Group is 
not yet committed to or significant future investments 
that will enhance the asset’s performance of the CGU 
being tested. The recoverable amount is sensitive to 
the discount rate used for the DCF model as well as 
the expected future cash-inflows and the growth rate 
used for extrapolation purposes. These estimates are 
most relevant to goodwill and other intangibles with 
indefinite useful lives recognised by the Group. The 
key assumptions used to determine the recoverable 
amount for the different CGUs, including a sensitivity 
analysis, are disclosed and further explained in note 4.
l)	
Leases - Estimating the Incremental 
Borrowing Rate
	
The Group cannot readily determine the interest rate 
implicit in the lease, therefore, it uses its incremental 
borrowing rate (IBR) to measure lease liabilities. The 
IBR is the rate of interest that the Group would have 
to pay to borrow over a similar term, and with a similar 
security, the funds necessary to obtain an asset of 
a similar value to the right-of-use asset in a similar 
economic environment. The IBR therefore reflects 
what the Group would have to pay, which requires 
estimation when no observable rates are available or 
when they need to be adjusted to reflect the terms 
and conditions of the lease. The Group estimates the 
IBR using observable inputs (such as market interest 
rates) when available.
	
Determining the lease term of contracts with 
renewal and termination options – Group as 
lessee
	
The Group determines the lease term as the non-
cancellable term of the lease, together with any 
periods covered by an option to extend the lease if it 
is reasonably certain to be exercised, or any periods 
covered by an option to terminate the lease, if it is 
reasonably certain not to be exercised.
	
The Group has several lease contracts that include 
extension and termination options. The Group applies 
judgement in evaluating whether it is reasonably 
certain whether or not to exercise the option to 
renew or terminate the lease. That is, it considers all 
relevant factors that create an economic incentive for 
it to exercise either the renewal or termination. After 
the commencement date, the Group reassesses the 
lease term if there is a significant event or change in 
circumstances that is within its control and affects 
its ability to exercise or not to exercise the option to 
renew or to terminate. Refer note 33.

Note 44 : The Labour Codes
On November 21, 2025, the Government of India notified provisions of the Code on Wages, 2019, the Industrial Relations 
Code, 2020, the Code on Social Security, 2020 and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, 
('Labour Codes') which consolidate twenty- nine existing labour laws into a unified framework governing employee 
benefits during employment and post employment. The Labour Codes, amongst other things introduces changes, 
including a uniform definition of wages and enhanced benefits relating to leave. The Group has assessed the financial 
implications of these changes which has resulted in increase in gratuity liability arising out of past service cost and 
increase in leave liability, in aggregate by ₹ 18.97 crores. Considering the impact arising out of an enactment of the new 
legislation is an event of non-recurring nature, the Group has presented this incremental amount as "Statutory impact 
of new Labour Codes" under "Exceptional Items" in the Statement of Profit and Loss for the year ended March 31, 2026. 
The Group continues to monitor the developments pertaining to Labour Codes and will evaluate impact if any on the 
measurement of liability pertaining to employee benefits.

10. Deduction of Tax
 
As you are aware that the Board of Directors of the 
Company, at its meeting held on May 15, 2026, have 
recommended a dividend at the rate of 10% equity per 
share i.e. H 0.10/- per Equity Share of face value Re. 1/- 
each fully paid-up for the Financial Year ended March 
31, 2026.
 
The dividend, as recommended by the Board, if 
approved at the ensuing annual general meeting, 
will be paid to the equity shareholders holding equity 
shares of the Company as at the record date i.e. Friday, 
July 10, 2026.
 
In accordance with the provisions of the Income-tax 
Act, 2025 (as amended by Finance Act, 2026) (‘the 
Act’), dividend paid or distributed by a Company, shall 
be taxable at the hands of shareholders. Accordingly, 
the Company is required to deduct tax at source from 
dividend paid to the shareholders, if approved at the 
Annual General Meeting (AGM) of the Company.
 
This communication provides a brief of the applicable 
Tax Deduction at Source (TDS) provisions under the Act 
for Resident and Non-Resident shareholder categories.
I. 
For Resident Shareholders:
 
Tax is required to be deducted at source under Section 
393(1) [Table Sr. No. 7] read with Section 393(4) [Table 
Sr. No. 10] of the Act, at the rate of 10% on the amount 
of dividend where shareholders have registered their 
valid Permanent Account Number (PAN). In case, 
shareholders do not have PAN / have not registered 
the

ir valid PAN details in their account, TDS at the rate 
of 20% shall be deducted under Section 397(2) of 
the Act.
a. 
Resident Individuals:
 
No tax shall be deducted on the dividend payable to 
resident individuals if:
 
i. 
Total dividend amount to be received by them 
during the Financial Year (FY) 2026-27 does not 
exceed H 10,000/; or
 
ii. 
The shareholder provides Form 121, provided 
that all the required eligibility conditions are met. 
Please note that all fields are mandatory to be 
filled up and Company may at its sole discretion 
reject the form if it does not fulfil the requirement 
of law. Format of Form 121 is enclosed herewith 
as Annexure-1.
 
iii. 
Exemption certificate, if any, issued by the 
Income-tax Department.
b. 
Resident Non-Individuals:
 
No tax shall be deducted on the dividend payable to the 
following resident non-individuals where they provide 
prescribed details and documents as per the format 
attached in Annexure-2.
 
i. 
Insurance Companies: Self declaration that 
it qualifies as ‘Insurer’ as per section 2(7A) of 
the Insurance Act, 1938 and has full beneficial 
interest with respect to the ordinary shares owned 
by it along with self-attested copy of PAN card 
and certificate of registration with Insurance 
Regulatory and Development Authority (IRDA)/ 
LIC/ GIC.

Mutual Funds: Self-declaration that it is registered

cess) on the amount of dividend payable to them. In 
case, non-resident shareholders provide a certificate 
issued under Section 395 of the Act, for lower/ 
Nil withholding of taxes, rate specified in the said 
certificate shall be considered, on submission of self-
attested copy of the same.
b. 
Further, as per Section 159 of the Act, the non-resident 
shareholder has the option to be governed by the 
provisions of the Double Tax Avoidance Treaty (DTAA) 
between India and the country of tax residence of the 
shareholder, if they are more beneficial to them. For this 
purpose, i.e., to avail Tax Treaty benefit, the non-resident 
shareholders are required to provide the following:
 
i. 
Self-attested copy of the PAN card allotted by 
the Indian Income Tax authorities.  In case, PAN 
is not available, the non-resident shareholder 
shall furnish (a) name, (b) email id, (c) contact 
number, (d) address in residency country, 
(e) Tax Identification Number of the residency 
country, format attached herewith as Annexure 3.
 
ii. 
Self-attested copy of Tax Residency Certificate 
(TRC) (for financial year April 1, 2026 to March 
31, 2027) obtained from the tax authorities of the 
country of which the shareholder is a resident.
 
iii. 
Copy of E-filed Form 41 (filed electronically on 
the Indian Income Tax web po

rtal pursuant to 
Notification no. 03/2022 dated July 16, 2022)

iv.

vi.

In terms of Regulation 23 of the Securities and Exchange 
Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure 
Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (“SEBI Listing 
Regulations, 2015”), as amended, material related 
p

arty transactions (“RPT”) require prior approval of the 
shareholders through ordinary resolutions, even if such 
transactions are in the ordinary course of business of the 
Company and at an arm’s length basis.
Pursuant to Regulation 23 read with Schedule XII of 
the SEBI Listing Regulations, 2015, as amended, RPT 
is considered material if the transaction(s), whether 
entered into individually or taken together with previous 
transactions during a financial year, exceeds 10% of the 
annual consolidated turnover of the Company as per its last 
audited financial statements, where the annual consolidated 
turnover of the Company is up to H 20,000 crore. Accordingly, 
the materiality threshold for seeking shareholders’ approval 
for related party transactions of the Company is H 940 crore.
Further, as per Regulation 2(1)(zc) of the SEBI Listing 
Regulations, 2015, the definition of RPT includes a 
transaction involving a transfer of resources, services or 
obligations between a listed entity or any of its subsidiaries 
on one hand and a related party of the listed entity or any of 
its subsidiaries on the other hand, regardless of whether a 
price is charged or not.
Accordingly, the Company is seeking the approval of the 
Members for the transactions proposed under Item Nos. 7 
and 8 of the accompanying Notice, as set out below.
Background, details and benefits of the transactions
Welspun Living Limited (“Company” or “WLL”) is a publicly 
listed company whose equity shares are listed and traded 
on BSE Limited and the National Stock Exchange of India 
Limited. The Company and its subsidiaries and associates 
(collectively, the “Welspun Living Group”) are engaged in 
the manufacture, marketing and sale of towels, rugs, bed 
sheets and other home textile products across various 
geographies and customer segments.
The Welspun Living Group operates through an integrated 
business model under which WLL and other entities within 
the group undertake manufacturing activities

, while 
Welspun Global Brands Limited (“WGBL”), a subsidiary 
of the Company, primarily undertakes marketing, brand 
management and distribution activities. WGBL markets and 
distributes products manufactured by the Welspun Living 
Group across international markets and services customers 
across retail, institutional and e-commerce segments.
Welspun USA Inc. (“WUSA”), a step-down subsidiary of 
the Company and a subsidiary of WGBL, operates as the 
Welspun Living Group’s business and distribution platform 
in the United States, which is one of its single largest 
export markets. WUSA provides six principal categories of 
services: (i) product sales facilitation, (ii) market analytics, 
(iii) design and product development support, (iv) supply-
chain management, (v) warehousing and (vi) customer 
relationship management. Through these activities, WUSA 
supports the Welspun Living Group’s relationships with 
customers in the United States and facilitates the distribution 
of products manufactured and/or marketed by the group.

Navigating the tariff headwinds
The sharp escalation in US tariff was the defining event 
of the year, and its impact was severe. About 59% of 
our revenue is US-facing. These partnerships have 
been built over decades and are central to our long-
term success. While protecting them came at a cost in 
the short term, but preserving trust and market position 
was the right strategic decision and we are convinced 
of that today.
Periods of disruptions often accelerate structural 
change. During the year, India strengthened its 
position as a preferred sourcing destination through 
progress on trade agreements with major economies, 
including the European Union and the United Kingdom 
as well as advancement of the India-US Bilateral 
Trade Agreem

ent. Meaningful movement across 
three of our most important export markets within a 
relatively short period has the potential to enhance 
India’s competitiveness and support long term growth 
prospects of the textile industry.
The EU and UK combined represent a home textile 
market worth over $30 billion. Combined with the 
ongoing diversification of global supply chains away 
from concentrated sourcing geographies, these 
agreements create a durable competitive advantage 
for India. What was once a cyclical opportunity is 
increasingly becoming a structural one.
Our efforts to diversify geographically also proved 
valuable during the year. Non-US revenues increased 
to 41% of total revenues, reflecting deliberate 
investments made over several years to broaden our 
market presence and reduce concentration risk. This 
diversification provided important resilience at a time 
when it was needed most.
Balance sheet strength as a 
strategic advantage
In a year marked by revenue pressure and volatility, 
financial discipline emerged as one of our greatest 
strengths. While the operating environment was 
challenging, our focus on cash generation, working 
capital efficiency and prudent capital allocation 
enabled us to strengthen the balance sheet and 
enhance financial flexibility. 
The outcomes were not incidental. They were the 
result of deliberate choices: maintaining capital 
discipline, optimising inventory, improving receivables 
management and directing resources towards the 
highest-value opportunities. In uncertain times, a 
strong balance sheet is more than a financial metric— 
it is a strategic advantage.
Our confidence in the long-term prospects of the 
business was also reflected in our capital allocation 
decisions. During the year, the Board approved a ₹252 
crore share buyback and a 10% dividend, underscoring 
our commitment to creating shareholder value while 
continuing to invest in future growth.
As the year progressed, early signs of recovery began

to emerge. In Q4 FY26, we delivered healthy sequential 
revenue growth and improvements in EBITDA margins. 
While there is more work ahead, the trajectory of the 
business is encouraging and reinforces our confidence 
in the path forward.

Building a consumer-led growth 
engine
For several years, we have articulated our ambition 
to become the FMCG of textiles—a company where 
brands, innovation and consumer relationships create 
enduring value alongside manufacturing excellence. 
FY26 marked an important step in that journey.
While our export business navigated significant tariff-
related disruption, our consumer-facing businesses 
demonstrated resilience and continued to grow. 
Domestic consumer revenues increased 9% to ₹657 
crore, while our branded and consumer portfolio 
contributed around one-fifth of the total revenue share. 
More importantly, these businesses provided stability 
in a year marked by external volatility, validating our 
strategy of building stronger consumer connections 
and diversified growth engines.
Our vision of 'Har Ghar Se Har Dil Tak Welspun' 
(From Every Home to Every Heart Welspun) gained 
meaningful traction during the year. The progress 
we witnessed was driven not merely by distribution 
expansion, but by increasing consumer preference, 
brand trust and product relevance.
Across global markets, our brand portfolio continued 
to strengthen their presence. Christy reinforced its 
position as a premium heritage brand while expanding 
into US through premium retailers and e-commerce 
and strengthening its presence across SEA and ANZ. 
Welhome scaled its footprint with strong traction across 
North America and expansion underway in UK and key 
Asian markets. We also accelerated our growth in the 
pillows segment, supported by higher utilisation at our 
Ohio facility and the commencement of operations at 
our Nevada facility, strengthening our manufacturing 
platform in the United States.

Our investment in US pillow manufacturing is not a 
response to tariffs alone. It represents a strategic entry 
into one of the fastest-growing categories within home 
textiles and reflects our broader approach of building 
growth platforms closer to the consumer. As we look 
ahead, brands, innovation and consumer engagement 
will increasingly complement manufacturing scale as 
key drivers of value creation.
Sustainability as a competitive 
moat
Sustainability is no longer just a responsibility; it 
is increasingly becoming a source of competitive 
advantage. In FY26, Welspun Living ranked #1 globally 
in ESG S&P Corporate Sustainability Assessment in 
Textiles, Apparels & Luxury goods category (as on 
11th Dec 2025). This reflects a sustained journey of 
improvement, with our score rising from 59 in FY23 to 
90 in FY26.
Our commitment to sustainability is closely linked to 
innovation. Our portfolio of over 50 patents, including 
products such as HygroCotton®, GX Pillow® and  
Wel-Trak®, contributed 22% of revenues during the 
year, demonstrating how responsible innovation can 
create meaningful business value.
As sustainability becomes a key consideration 
in sourcing decisions for global retailers, our 
leadership position strengthens customer trust, 
enhances differentiation and reinforces our long-
term competitiveness.
Our people
Throughout FY26, our people remained the 
foundation of our resilience and progress. While many 
organisations responded to uncertainty by reducing 
workforce capacity, we chose to preserve the talent, 
capabilities and institutional knowledge that have been 
built over decades. We believe long-term success 
is driven not only by financial capital, but also by 
human capital.
We earned the Great Place to Work® certification for 
the second consecutive year, reflecting our continued 
focus on building a culture of trust, growth and 
inclusion. Women now constitute more than 35% of our 
workforce, among the highest representation level

s in 
the industry.
Our SPUN initiative continued to create meaningful 
impact by transforming factory waste into livelihood 
opportunities for rural women artisans, demonstrating 
how sustainability and social inclusion can go hand 
in hand.

Economic review   
Global economy
The global economy entered a new phase in 2025, 
marked by the simulta

neous pursuit of growth, 
resilience and strategic realignment. While global 
GDP grew by 3.4%1,  the operating environment was 
increasingly shaped by changing trade policies, 
geopolitical developments and the reconfiguration of 
global supply chains. Businesses across industries 
increasingly balanced efficiency with resilience 
as governments sought to strengthen economic 
security, diversify sourcing networks and recalibrate 
trade partnerships.
Against this backdrop, the most consequential 
development for export-oriented sectors was the 
emergence of a new global trade architecture. The 
escalation of US tariff measures and the acceleration 
of bilateral and regional trade negotiations signalled a 
structural reset in market access and competitiveness. 
For India, progress on trade agreements with key 
markets, including the United Kingdom and the 
European Union, alongside ongoing trade engagement 
with the United States, has the potential to redefine 
export opportunities and strengthen the country's 
position within global supply chains. 
Advanced economies: Moderation amid 
policy tightness
In the United States, resilient consumer spending drove 
growth to 2.0% in 2025, with a projected increase to 
2.4% in 2026. The US Dollar maintained its strength 
through safe-haven demand and divergent monetary 
policies. This lowered import costs for US consumers, 
tightened global liquidity and increased transaction 
costs for emerging markets. Meanwhile, the US labour 
market remained stable, with unemployment projected 
to hover around 4% through 2026.2 
Emerging markets: Sustained momentum
Emerging markets expanded by 4.4% in 2025 and are 
projected to stabilise at 4.2% and 4.1% in 2026 and 
2027, respectively, driven by resilient domestic demand 
and robust investment. In China, GDP grew by 5.0% 
in 2025 and is forecast at 4.5% for 2026, supported 
by manufacturing stimulus. However, escalating 
trade frictions and shifting tariff policies continue to 
complica

te Chinese export dynamics, accelerating 
global supply chain diversification toward more stable 
manufacturing hubs.3
Inflation: Although easing remains above 
target levels 
Inflationary pressures showed signs of gradual 
moderation during the year. Global headline inflation is 
estimated at 4.1% in 2025 and projected to ease to 3.8% 
in 2026, supported by improving supply conditions and 
stabilising commodity prices.4	
 
However, inflation remains above target levels of 2%-
6% in several economies, prompting central banks to 
maintain relatively tight monetary policies. This has 
continued to influence global liquidity conditions and 
growth prospects.
In the US, easing tariff tensions with China and 
improvements in global supply chains have helped 
moderate inflation. Inflation is expected to decline to 
approximately 2.6% in 2026, while fading tariff effects 
and lower oil prices should bring core PCE inflation 
back to 2% during the first half of 2027.

Global cotton fundamentals: Production, 
demand and pricing
The global cotton market remained steady but subdued 
through the 2025–26 season, balancing an expanded 
agricultural output against a measured downstream 
consumption profile. According to the USDA, global 
cotton production is estimated at 121.9 million 
bales (nearly 26 million tonnes), reflecting a year-
on-year uptick driven by higher acreage, improving 
yields, and stable input conditions across primary 
producing nations like China, India, Brazil, and the US.6   
Conversely, global consumption is projected at a more 
moderate 119.1 million bales, resulting in a marginal 
production surplus that has built up global inventories 
and kept overall market pricing under pressure.7  
China and India continue to anchor global demand, 
co

llectively accounting for over half of global mill 
consumption. However, Chinese buying remained 
cautious due to ongoing trade frictions, slower export 
orders, and structural supply chain shifts. Reflecting 
these international linkages, the Indian domestic 
market experienced varied pricing across regional 
grades; according to the Cotton Association of India 
(CAI), upcountry spot prices for standard categories 
successfully stabilised between ₹54,000 and ₹60,600 
per candy in March 2026, depending on staple length 
and quality specifications.8  Moving forward, the 
global cotton matrix is expected to remain structurally 
sound and broadly stable, supported by a gradual 
normalisation of global trade flows and steady demand 
anchoring from the Indian and Chinese textile hubs.

This momentum was reinforced by new structural 
frameworks, including the National Fibre Scheme,

the Tex-Eco Initiative, solidifying the state's focus on 
modernisation, sustainable manufacturing, and long-
term export competitiveness.
Exports and trade performance
India’s textile and apparel export ecosystem 
demonstrated strong resilience, expanding by 2.1% to 
reach ₹3,16,334.9 crore, up from ₹3,09,859.3 crore in

reciprocal tariff regime, whic

h temporarily squeezed

Crucially for diversified manufacturers, this steady

geographic expansion, with growth recorded across 
more than 120 destinations, led by notable surges in 
the UAE (22.3%), Spain (15.5%), and the UK (7.8%).19 
This broad-based market footprint, paired with the 
structural extension of government support mechanisms 
such as the RoSCTL and RoDTEP schemes beyond 
March 2026, ensures a highly predictable regulatory 
and margin framework. This stability empowers scaled, 
vertically integrated market leaders to aggressively 
capture shifting global sourcing shares while insulating 
themselves from localised supply chain disruptions.

India-UK Free 
Trade Agreement
Effective 15 July 2026, the India–UK 
Comprehensive Economic and Trade 
Agreement (CETA) grants duty-free 
access to 99% of Indian exports to the 
UK, including textiles, apparel and home 
textiles, eliminating the 10–12% tariffs 
that previously applied to many of these 
products. The agreement significantly 
enhances the price competitiveness 
of Indian exporters in one of their key 
developed markets, creating opportunities 
for higher exports, greater investment and 
deeper integration into UK supply chains. 
Beyond tariff liberalisation, the FTA is 
expected to strengthen bilateral trade and 
investment, remove long-standing post-
Brexit trade barriers, and support the long-
term expansion of India's textile and apparel 
sector.22
•	 Levelling the playing field: India 
can finally match the Duty-free 
status enjoyed by Pakistan and 
Bangladesh. This is expected 
to trigger a volume surge in the 
textile categories.
•	 Design collaboration: The FTA 
encourages design houses in 
the UK to partner with Indian 
mills. This facilitates a shift from 
‘Contract Manufacturing’ (OEM) to 
‘Design-led Manufacturing’ (ODM), 
increasing the brand value of 
Indian exports.
•	 Retail partnership stability: 
Major UK retailers can now sign 
three- to five-year multi-billion-
dollar sourcing contracts with 
Indian mills without fearing sudden 
tariff hikes.

Textile and apparel industry 
Global textile and apparel industry
The global textile market witnessed steady expansion, 
supported by rising demand across apparel, home 
furnishings and technical textiles. The market size 
was estimated at $2,123.72 billion in 2025 and is 
projected to reach $2,281.51 billion in 2026. It is further 
anticipated to grow to approximately $4,016.50 billion 
by 2034, registering a CAGR of 7.35% from 2025 to 
2034.31 
The global apparel market was valued at around 
$1.9 trillion in 2025 and is expected to grow to 
approximately $2.3 trillion by 2030, reflecting a CAGR 
of around 4%, even as the industry contends with cost 
pressures, evolving consumer demand and supply 
chain diversification. The US remained the largest 
apparel market globally, while emerging economies, 
especially China and India, continued to drive growth.32 
Global textile and apparel trade
Global textile and apparel trade, estimated at 
approximately $900 billion in 2025, underwent its most 
significant structural disruption in decades during FY26. 
The escalation of US tariffs on Indian textiles to 50%, 
followed by the India-US trade reset and landmark 
trade agreements with EU and UK FTA to provide zero-
duty access, has triggered a fundamental realignment 
of global sourcing patterns. India, the world’s 
largest cotton producer and a vertically integrated 
manufacturing powerhouse, is emerging as the primary 
beneficiary of t

his ‘China Plus One’ acceleration.
India's value chain dominance
As the world’s largest cotton producer, India stands 
out as a completely vertically integrated manufacturing 
powerhouse. Controlling the value chain from raw fibre 
to finished product allows India to serve as the primary 
strategic beneficiary of global vendor migration. 
Apparel was the largest traded category, accounting for 
approximately 60% in 2025.

Highlights of Union Budget FY2742  
The Union Budget for FY27 reinforces India's 
industrial manufacturing focus, directly 
supporting organised textile enterprises through 
targeted fiscal allocations and scale-driven 
infrastructure developments:
•	 Enhanced fiscal allocation: The Ministry of 
Textiles has been allocated ₹5,279 crore for 
FY27, up from the revised allocation of ₹5,272 
crore in FY26. This sustained budgetary support 
anchors the government’s ambitious Vision 
2030, which aims to scale national textile exports 
from approximately ₹3 lakh crore to ₹9 lakh 
crore ($100 billion) through enhanced domestic 
capability and expanded global market access.
•	 Integrated programme for the Textile sector: 
The budget introduces a comprehensive 
Integrated Programme to strengthen the entire 
fibre-to-finished product value chain. The 
Tex-Eco Initiative, which provides structural 
incentives for sustainable manufacturin

g, 
circularity, and green product development, 
directly validates and accelerates the advanced 
ESG and sustainable home textile pipeline.
•	 PM MITRA Parks infrastructure scale: The 
budget continues to accelerate the rollout of 
seven PM MITRA (Mega Integrated Textile Region 
and Apparel) Parks, backed by an approved 
₹4,445 crore central investment through FY28. 
Designed to attract cumulative capital inflows of 
₹27,434 crore, this mega-infrastructure model 
lowers logistics friction, establishes world-class 
manufacturing clusters, and provides structured 
cost efficiencies that bolster the global 
competitiveness of large-scale exporters.

Indian home textiles industry
The Indian home textile industry maintained steady 
growth throughout FY26, propelled by resilient export 
volumes, structural inventory normalisation across 
major international retail chains, and an accelerating 
global pivot toward ‘China+1’ sourcing strategies. 
Industry revenues expanded by

6-8% in FY26, while 
operating profit margins successfully stabilised within 
a healthy 14% to 15% range, supported by predictable 
raw material procurement costs and favourable 
exchange rate realisations.46 
The United States stands as the premier destination for 
Indian home textile exports, commanding a significant 
48% share of total outbound shipments.47 India further 
reinforced its global leadership position, accounting for 
approximately 45% of global cotton terry towel imports 
and 60% of cotton sheet imports into the United States, 
making it the single largest sourcing origin for these 
categories.48 
Looking ahead, this structural dominance is positioned 
to strengthen further. The progressive normalisation of 
trade terms, paired with the imminent operationalisation 
of milestone bilateral trade pacts, headlined by the 
India-UK and India-EU Free Trade agreement (FTA), 
presents a highly lucrative growth runway, unlocking 
duty-free market access to high-potential European 
zones. Over the long term, the Indian home textile 
ecosystem is projected to expand at a robust 8.9% 
CAGR, scaling from a baseline valuation of $10.78 
billion in 2023 to reach $23.32 billion by 2032, 
driven by institutional global vendor diversification 
and a permanent consumer preference shift toward 
innovative, sustainable, and traceable premium textile 
solutions.49  
Technical textile industry
Global technical textile industry
Technical textiles are gaining increasing importance 
due to their functional properties of mechanical 
strength, thermal resistance, durability and 
performance efficiency, rather than aesthetic appeal. 
The growth of the sector is further supported by rising 
demand across industries of automotive, healthcare, 
construction and agriculture, along with increasing 
investments in advanced materials and sustainable 
textile solutions. 
The technical textiles market experienced robust 
growth during the year under review, growing from 
$251.02 billion

in 2025. Projected to reach $264.42 
billion in 2026, reflecting a CAGR of 5.3%, the market 
is expected to maintain its growth trajectory and 
expand further to $329.23 billion by 2030, with a 
modest acceleration in CAGR to 5.6% over the period.50 
Synthetic polymers/fibres constitute the largest share 
of the technical textile market, owing to their superior 
strength, durability, flexibility and cost efficiency. At 
the same time, natural fibres are expected to witness 
gradual growth, supported by increasing demand for 
sustainable and eco-friendly materials.
For Welspun Living, these trends present a compelling 
opportunity to strengthen its presence in the 
nonwoven technical textiles segment. Backed by India's 
largest spunlace capacity and advanced Spunlace, 
Needlepunch and Thermal Bonding technologies, the 
Company is well positioned to address the increasing 
need for high-performance and sustainable technical 
textile solutions.
Technical textile by regions
The Asia-Pacific region continues to be the primary 
engine of growth for the global technical textiles 
market, accounting for a dominant 46% revenue share 
in 2025.51

Flooring industry 
Global flooring industry
The global floor covering market was valued at $245.75 
billion in 2025 and is expected to grow to $256.24 
billion in 2026 and $312.42 billion by 2031, growing at a 
CAGR of 4.04% from 2026 onwards.55 
Product innovation, particularly in vinyl and rigid-core 
formats favoured for their moisture resistance and 
quick installation are driving growth. While residential 
demand remains steady, commercial sectors, led by 
healthcare and education, are increasing the need for 
durable, hygienic surfaces. Additionally, as companies 
navigate tariff pressures, supply chains are becoming 
more regionalised, with increased domestic production 
helping stabilise costs and shorten lead times.
Regional Insights
The global flooring industry in 2025 continued to 
evolve around sustainable materials, resilient supply 
chains, and localised manufacturing, even as growth 
moderated across certain geographies. 
Regional demand profiles shifted significantly: North 
America’s market was heavily sustained by home 
renovation and remodelling activity, with US home 
improvement spend

ing exceeding $400 billion, as 
elevated mortgage rates temporarily disincentivised 
new housing construction.56 In Europe, growth was 
primarily driven by strict sustainability mandates and 
regulatory frameworks like the Renovation Wave, which 
accelerated the adoption of low-emission, recyclable, 
and energy-efficient materials.57 Conversely, the Asia-
Pacific region remains the largest and fastest-growing 
market, commanding a dominant 37% global market 
share due to rapid urbanisation, public infrastructure 
development, and vast urban renewal initiatives, 
such as China’s 60,000-project modernisation 
programme.58,59 Together, these distinct regional 
dynamics underscore a global transition toward 
durability, eco-conscious product engineering, and 
optimised regional supply chains.

Company review 
Welspun Living Limited is a part of the Welspun world, 
one of India’s fastest-growing global conglomerates 
with diversified businesses spanning line pipes, home 
textile products, infrastructure, warehousing, steel,

including Welspun and Spaces.

and Endurance, Welspun remains focused on creating 
smarter, more sustainable living spaces worldwide.

Key business and operational highlights
FY26 was a year shaped by global trade disruptions, 
tariff un

certainties, geopolitical tensions, and evolving 
consumer demand. Despite these external headwinds, 
Welspun Living demonstrated resilience through 
disciplined execution, strong customer partnerships, 
operational agility and strategic diversification.
Consolidated revenues for FY26 stood at ₹9,468 
crore, while EBITDA margins for the year stood at 9.1%. 
The Company remained focused on protecting long-
term customer relationships, strengthening operating 
efficiencies, and preserving financial discipline 
through a challenging cycle. Focused working capital 
optimisation and prudent capital allocation led to strong 
free cash flow generation and a sharp reduction in net 
debt during the year.
Management actions through FY26 remained deliberate 
and forward-looking. The Company accelerated 
geographic diversification, with the non-US business 
contribution expanding to ~41%, while continuing to 
invest in innovation, sustainability, branded businesses, 
and nearshore manufacturing capabilities. The year also 
marked the commencement of commercial production 
at Welspun Living’s Nevada greenfield pillow facility 
in the US, strengthening its long-term presence in the 
global sleep ecosystem.
India’s strengthening position as a preferred sourcing 
destination, supported by evolving trade frameworks 
with the US, UK, EU, Japan, and Australia, is creating 
significant long-term opportunities for the textile sector. 
Against this backdrop, Welspun Living’s diversified 
portfolio, branded offerings, integrated supply chain 
capabilities, innovation platforms, and sustainability 
leadership continue to strengthen its position as a 
preferred partner for leading global retailers.
The domestic consumer business remained a key 
growth driver during the year, with revenues growing 
~9% YoY, supported by stronger brand traction, 
premiumisation, and channel diversification. The 
Company’s global brands, including Christy and 
Welhome, continued to deepen presence across 
inte

rnational markets, while sustainability leadership 
was reinforced through Welspun Living being ranked 
#1 globally in the 2025 S&P Global Corporate 
Sustainability Assessment for the Textile, Apparel & 
Luxury Goods category.
Backed by strong customer relationships, sustainability-
led operations, and disciplined execution, Welspun 
Living enters FY27 with a strengthened balance 
sheet, improving market positioning, and confidence 
in its ability to capture the next phase of growth 
opportunities globally.

Risk categories and mitigation
Risk category
Mitigation strategies
US tariffs and  
market concentration
Multiple FTAs with the European Union, UK and New Zealand are expected to effectively mitigate 
risks arising from tariff-impacted geographies. We are also working to deepen our presence by 
developing partnerships across new markets such as Australia, New

Zealand, GCC countries and 
Japan. In addition, we continue to diversify our channels across Retail, Hospitality and E-commerce, 
while expanding into new product categories and strengthening our portfolio of licenced and owned 
brands.
Geopolitical uncertainty
We continue to diversify our market presence to reduce dependence on any single geography. Our 
expansion plans are focused on Europe, the UK, Japan and the wider APAC region. We maintain 
long-term contracts with suppliers and adequate cotton coverage of more than 4–5 months to 
support supply continuity. Management closely monitors evolving geopolitical developments and 
takes necessary steps to ensure uninterrupted availability of raw materials.
Major raw materials 
availability and pricing 
(Cotton/Fabric/Yarn)
Procurement plans are prepared well in advance, and we maintain adequate cotton coverage of 
approximately 4–5 months. Global cotton market developments are monitored through a structured 
review process supported by active coordination with the marketing team and various market 
intelligence tools. Safety stock levels have been reassessed to address higher lead times for 
imported cotton. We continue to increase the use of recycled cotton to optimise production costs 
while advancing sustainability objectives. Recycled cotton usage has increased to 20% over the last 
year compared to less than 15% previously. In addition, we have installed a cotton fibre recycling 
plant with a capacity of 4–5 tonnes per day at Anjar, which is now operational.
Exposure to volatility in 
foreign exchange rates
We have a robust foreign exchange policy in place to manage currency volatility, supported by 
continuous monitoring and periodic adjustment of hedge positions to facilitate timely corrective 
action.
Risk arising from 
inadequate 
attraction and retention of 
talent
We continue to invest in upskilling initiatives to enhance productivity and workforce capability, while 
implementing focused measures to attrac

t, develop and retain skilled talent. Succession plans have 
also been established for all critical management positions.
ESG-related risks
A Board-level ESG and CSR Committee has been constituted to oversee, monitor and drive ESG and 
CSR initiatives across the organisation. We continue to implement our Board-approved roadmap 
towards carbon neutrality and remain focused on achieving 100% renewable energy by 2030, 
freshwater positivity by 2030, zero waste to landfill by 2027, 100% sustainable cotton sourcing by 
2030 and enhanced biodiversity outcomes.
Challenges in maintaining 
growth in a competitive 
domestic and global 
environment
We consistently drive innovation to strengthen our competitive position and have diversified our 
business through Direct-to-Customer channels, alongside a stronger focus on the Indian domestic 
market. Expansion into adjacent businesses such as Advanced Textiles and Flooring has further 
supported risk diversification and sustainable business growth.

Background:
 
Nomination and Remuneration Committee ("NRC") 
has laid down the criteria for evaluation of performance 
of the Board, its committees and the directors.
 
In compliance with Sections 134, 178 of, and Para II, 
V and VIII of Schedule IV to, the Act and Regulation 17 
of Para A of Part D of Schedule II to the SEBI Listing 
Regulations, 2015, the annual performance evaluation 
of the Board, its Committees and individual Directors 
was carried out during the year. In order to facilitate 
an objective and independent evaluation process, the 
Company engaged an external professional agency 
to conduct the evaluation exercise. The evaluation 
framework, including the revised questionnaires and 
evaluation criteria, was reviewed by the Nomination 
and Remuneration Committee before being circulated 
to the Directors for providing their ratings and 
feedback in a confidential manner.
 
Mode of evaluation:
 
Your Company has developed an in-house digital 
platform to facilitate confidential responses to 
a structured questionnaire.Each question in the 
evaluation was rated on a fivepoint scale, ranging 
from the lowest rating ("1") to the highest rating ("5").
 
The evaluation criteria covered various aspects 
relating to the functioning and effectiveness of the 
Board, Committees and Directors, including Board 
composition and competencies, strategic oversight, 
governance and compliance, risk management, 
Board dynamics, participation in discussions, quality 
of decision-making, stakeholder engagement and 
effectiveness of processes and procedures. The 
evaluation criteria were broadly aligned with the 
applicable regulatory requirements and governance 
be

st practices.
 
The Independent Directors, at their separate meeting, 
reviewed the performance of the Non-Independent 
Directors, the Chairperson and the Board as a whole, 
taking into account the views of the Executive and 
Non-Executive Directors. Further, the Nomination and 
Remuneration Committee reviewed the performance 
evaluation outcome of the Board, Committees and 
individual Directors. Thereafter, the Board reviewed 
and discussed the evaluation outcome and noted 
the suggestions for further strengthening the overall 
effectiveness of the Board and its Committees.
 
Results:
 
The outcome of the evaluation confirmed that 
the Board and its Committees continue to operate 
effectively, demonstrating strong governance, 
strategic leadership, sound oversight, professionalism, 
ethical conduct, effective stakeholder engagement 
and robust risk management.
 
The evaluation acknowledged the Board's diverse 
composition, the appropriate blend of functional, 
industry and financial expertise, and the constructive 
participation of Directors, all of which contributed to 
effective deliberations, balanced decision-making 
and overall Board effectiveness. It also recognised 
the Board's strong commitment to ethics, integrity, 
compliance, transparency and long-term value 
creation for all stakeholders.
 
The evaluation further highlighted the effective 
leadership of the Chairperson in fostering an 
environment of open dialogue, constructive 
discussion and collaborative decision-making. The 
Committees were also assessed as performing 
effectively, with appropriate focus on their respective 
responsibilities and governance oversight, supported 
by well-structured processes and disciplined 
meeting management.
 
The evaluation also identified opportunities for further 
enhancement, particularly in strengthening long-term 
strategic oversight and review mechanisms.

Executive Summary of report on Impact Assessment 
of CSR Project (Assessment was carried out by 
Protiviti)
 
A. 
Executive Summary
 
 
Protiviti conducted the impact assessment for 
eight CSR projects for FY 2024-25, covering 
WelKrishi, Welspun Super Sports Women, 
WelNetrutva, WelPrakruti, WelShiksha, 
WelSuraksha, WelSwasthya and WelDisha. 
The evaluation covered 1,002 intervention 
beneficiaries and 325 control or non-
beneficiaries wherever applicable, and was 
conducted at a significance level of 90% 
confidence and 5% margin of error. In addition 
to primary beneficiaries, other key stakeholders 
were also interviewed to strengthen the 
as

sessment and triangulate findings.
 
 
The evaluation was structured around the IRECS 
framework, which assessed Inclusiveness, 
Relevance, Effectiveness, Convergence and 
Sustainability. The assessment focused on 
understanding the extent to which desired 
outcomes and impacts were achieved, whether 
project outputs were effectively and efficiently 
delivered by implementation teams, the potential 
risks and opportunities in each project, and the 
success stories and recommendations that can 
inform future programming.
 
 
A qualitative approach was used for drawing 
inferences on outcomes and impact among target 
beneficiaries. The evaluation tools included 
Key Informant’s Interview Questionnaire, Fixed 
Group Discussion and Observation checklists.

The combination of beneficiary consultations, 
control group comparisons wherever applicable 
and stakeholder interviews provided a broad 
evidence base for understanding both immediate 
outputs and visible changes generated through 
the CSR projects.
 
 
Across thematic areas, the CSR program 
demonstrated visible improvements in 
education, healthcare, road safety, livelihoods, 
agriculture, environment, women’s sports and 
skill development. The education interventions 
contributed to improved learning outcomes, 
digital skills, career awareness, classroom 
participation and athlete support. The healthcare 
interventions improved health awareness, 
access to care, health-seeking behaviour, 
nutritional intake and reduced out-of-pocket 
expenditure. Road safety interventions improved 
awareness, emergency response readiness, 
understanding of the Good Samaritan Law 
and healthcare access for drivers. Livelihood 
interventions strengthened employable skills, 
income generation, enterprise creation, women’s 
financial decision-making and farm productivity. 
Agriculture and environment interventions 
contributed to better yield bands, soil health, 
water

-use efficiency, reduced stalk burning, 
expanded green cover, water storage capacity, 
community ownership and environmental 
awareness. The women empowerment and skill 
development interventions supported athletes’ 
performance, rankings, resilient comebacks, 
job readiness, confidence, placement-linked 
training and early income generation among 
placed beneficiaries.
 
B. 
Scope of work and Evaluation Coverage
 
 
The scope of work covered eight CSR projects 
for FY 2025-26. WelNetrutva covered 210 
intervention beneficiaries and 80 control 
beneficiaries across Telangana, Gujarat, Uttar 
Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh. WelSwasthya 
covered 160 intervention beneficiaries and 80 
control beneficiaries across Telangana, Gujarat, 
Madhya Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. WelShiksha 
covered 180 intervention beneficiaries and 80 
control beneficiaries across Telangana, Gujarat 
and Madhya Pradesh. WelKrishi covered 178 
intervention beneficiaries and 85 control 
beneficiaries across Gujarat and Maharashtra.
 
 
The evaluation also covered WelDisha with 
40 intervention beneficiaries in Telangana, 
WelSuraksha with 100 intervention beneficiaries 
across Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, 
WelPrakruti with 100 intervention beneficiaries 
across Telangana, Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh, 
and Welspun Super Sports Women with 34 
intervention beneficiaries across pan-India 
locations. Overall, the evaluation reached 1,002 
intervention beneficiaries and 325 control or 
non-beneficiary respondents. Other relevant 
stakeholders were also interviewed to provide 
additional context on implementation, outcomes 
and future opportunities.
 
C. 
Evaluation Framework and Methodology
 
 
The IRECS framework was used as the evaluation 
lens. Inclusiveness assessed the extent to 
which the projects ensured that vulnerable 
stakeholders equitably benefitted from 
interventions. Relevance assessed whether 
project interventions were equipped to address 
the priority needs of targeted stakeholders.

Effectiveness assessed the extent to which 
desired project outcomes were achieved by 
making the best possible use of available 
resources. Convergence assessed the extent 
to which projects collaborated with external 
stakeholders and leveraged resources for project 
outputs and outcomes. Sustainability assessed 
whether the benefits of the projects continued or 
were likely to continue after project exit.
 
 
The evaluation objectives were to assess 
achievement of desired outcomes and impact, 
examine whether outputs were delivered 
effectively and efficiently by implementation 
teams, identify potential risks and opportunities 
across the projects, and document success 
stories and recommendations for future 
programming. The evaluation adopted a 
qualitative approach for drawing inferences on 
outcomes and impact on target beneficiaries, 
supported by Key Informant’s Interview 
Questionnaire, Fixed Group Discussion and 
Observation checklists. The sample included 
1,002 intervention respondents and 325 control 
respondents, with significance set at 90% 
confidence and 5% margin of error.

through kitchen gardens, enabled 2,170 
farmers to adopt drip and sprinkler irrigation

g) 
Environment – WelPrakruti - WelPrakruti 
promoted environmental sustainability, 
climate resilience and community well-
being through sapling distribution and 
the construction and rejuvenation of farm 
ponds. The program distributed and planted 
12,000+ saplings across Gujarat, Madhya 
Pradesh and Telangana, with a focus on 
fruit-bearing, medicinal and native species. 
It created and rejuvenated farm ponds 
across nine sites in Gujarat, adding water 
storage capacity on Panchayat land. The 
program implemented a household-led 
caregiving model for sapling maintenance, 
conducted community awareness sessions 
on water conservation, waste management 
and natural farming practices, supported 
government schools with kitchen 
gardens, dustbins and waste management 
awareness, and developed a biodiversity-
rich Nature Park at Welspun Anjar with 167 
plant species, walking trails, water bodies 
and demonstration plots for sustainable 
plantation techniques.
 
 
 
The program increased green cover and 
supported over 2,300 community members 
across Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh and 
Telangana with household-level plantation. 
The household-based caregiving system 
strengthened community ownership and 
contributed to high survival rates. The 
plantation of 12,000+ trees created the 
potential to absorb approximately 264

metric tonnes of carbon dioxide annually, 
generate approximately 1,416 tonnes of 
oxygen annually, remove approximately 54 
tonnes of air pollutants annually at maturity 
and intercept and retain approximately 
34 million litres of rainwater annually. The 
creation and rejuvenation of farm ponds 
generated storage capacity of 1.20 lakh 
cubic metres, improving year-round water 
availability for livestock and nearby farms. 
The Nature Park enhanced green cover, 
groundwater recharge potential, water 
storage capacity and biodiversity, while also 
serving as a recreational and educational 
space for community members.
 
 
 
Going forward, the program should 
expand partnerships with panchayats 
and government schemes to scale water 
conservation efforts further. It may also 
consider onboarding a knowledge partner 
on water security and should monitor 
groundwater-related impacts.
	
	
h) 
Women Empowerment - Welspun Super 
Sports Women - Welspun Super Sports 
Women provided sustained financial, 
technical and holistic support to female 
athletes to enable them to compete at 
the highest levels and achieve sporting 
excellence. The program supported 22 
women athletes from more than 12 sporting 
disciplines. Support included equipment, 
training and recovery, event participation 
costs related to travel and logistics, and 
responses to immediate and urgent needs. 
Beyond financial aid, the program also 
provided mental health support through 
sports psychologists, customised nutrition 
plans for endurance athletes and media and 
social engagement activities.
 
 
 
The program contributed to strong medal 
performance across levels. Athletes 
supported under WSSW collectively won 
85 medals, including 35 gold, 21 silver and 
29 bronze medals across state, national 
and international competitions, with 45 
medals secured at international events 
during FY 2024-25. The program also 
supported world championship podium 
finishes, including Palak Kohli’s bronze in

i) 
Skill Development – WelDisha - WelDisha 
aimed to enhance employability and improve 
livelihood opportunities for youth through 
placement-linked, industry-relevant skill 
training. The program provided Data Entry 
Operator training to 21 beneficiaries in 
Telangana, including 4 male and 17 female 
trainees, through classroom and hands-on 
computer lab sessions. It also delivered Retail 
Sales Executive training to 20 beneficiaries, 
including 9 male and 11 female trainees, 
using a specialised retail simulation lab. 
A dedicated training centre with modern 
classrooms and specialised laboratories 
supported practical and industry-relevant 
learning. Employability and soft-skills 
training in basic English, workplace 
behaviour, professionalism, grooming and 
ti

me management was provided to all 41 
trainees, along with placement support 
activities including employer linkages and 
interview coordination.
 
 
 
At the time of evaluation, 15% of beneficiaries 
had been placed across various companies. 
Placed beneficiaries were earning ₹10,000 
to ₹15,000 per month, contributing to 
improved household financial stability. 
Beneficiaries demonstrated improved 
technical competencies and strengthened 
soft skills, including communication, 
workplace behavior professionalism and 
time management. Exposure to structured 
training and practical labs also increased 
beneficiaries’ confidence to navigate formal 
work environments.
 
 
 
Going forward, the program should re-
evaluate the feasibility of undertaking skill 
development trainings internally or consider 
deferring further implementation until 
ongoing challenges and final placement 
outcomes have been fully evaluated.
 
E. 
Consolidated Way Forward
 
 
The evaluation points to a set of cross-domain 
priorities for future programming. First, Welspun 
should scale and replicate proven models, 
including expansion of successful coding clubs 
and smart classes, farmer-focused livelihood 
services in nearby underserved regions, and 
water conservation interventions through 
panchayat and government partnerships. 
Second, convergence and partnerships should 
be strengthened with RTOs, traffic police, 
schools, panchayats, government schemes and 
potential knowledge partners to improve reach, 
continuity and technical rigour.
 
 
Third, transition and sustainability planning 
should be improved. This includes transferring 
para-teacher skills and methodologies to regular 
government teachers and establishing planned 
exit frameworks for athletes transitioning out 
of WSSW. Fourth, service quality and targeting 
should be deepened by phasing down program 
intensity in mature health locations, redirecting 
resources to underserved geographies, and 
expanding community-based N

CD screening, 
follow-up, referral and malnutrition modules.
 
 
Fifth, market and finance linkages should be 
strengthened for women livelihood beneficiaries, 
particularly in geographies where training-to-
income conversion has been limited. Sixth, 
program data should be more systematically 
used for decision-making. Source Trace data 
should be used for strategic decision-making, 
market engagement and risk management, and 
skill training trades should be selected based on 
market studies and demand assessments. Finally, 
the program should re-evaluate the feasibility of 
undertaking skill development training internally 
or defer further implementation until ongoing 
challenges and final placement outcomes have 
been fully evaluated.

as a trustee and assumes fiduciary responsibility to 
protect the interests of the Company, its members,

beyond compliance and reflects a commitment 
to ethical conduct, integrity, transparency, 
accountability, and responsible decision-
making. The Board supports the core principles 
of good governance and recognizes their critical 
role in building and maintaining investor and 
stakeholder trust.
	
The Company emphasizes robust governance 
frameworks, effective oversight, clear disclosures, 
and strong internal controls. The Board and 
Management are committed to upholding both the 
letter and spirit of applicable laws, regulations, and 
governance best practices.
	
The Board and Management are committed to 
complying with the letter and spirit of applicable 
laws and regulations, including the Securities and 
Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and 
Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (“the

ions, 2015”). Strong governance

reviewed and strengthened to align with evolving 
regulatory requirements and best in class standards, 
thereby supporting long term value creation and 
sustainable business success.
	
CODE OF GOVERNANCE:
	
Corporate Governance at Welspun extends beyond 
compliance—it is a fundamental philosophy that 
guides the way we operate. It is central to strengthening 
transparency, promoting comprehensive disclosures, 
and ensuring accountability across the organization.
	
All Directors and employees adhere to a Code of 
Conduct that establishes the Company’s policies on 
key matters, including relationships with customers, 
suppliers, contract manufacturers, shareholders, and 
government authorities. The Company is supported 
by an effective and diverse Board that defines the 
principles guiding our day-to-day operations. Robust 
systems and procedures are in place to ensure 
adherence to the highest standards of governance 
and best practices.
	
Governance Structure
	
Welspun has established a robust and transparent 
governance framework that promotes ethical 
conduct, accountability, and long term value creation. 
The governance structure is built around the Board of 
Directors, its Committees, and the Senior Management 
Team, ensuring effective oversight, compliance with 
applicable laws and regulations, and adoption of best 
in class governance practices.
	
Board of Directors
	
The Board of Directors is the apex governing authority 
of the Company and bears overall responsibility for 
its strategic direction, governance, and performance. 
Acting in a fiduciary capacity, the Board provides 
strategic guidance, ensures integrity of financial 
and non financial disclosures, and oversees the 
effectiveness of internal controls, risk manageme

nt 
systems, and compliance mechanisms. The Board 
also formulates key policies and monitors their 
implementation across the organization.
	
Committees of the Board
	
The Board has constituted various Committees to 
focus on specific areas of governance in accordance 
with statutory requirements and approved charters. 
These Committees assist the Board by providing 
specialized oversight and recommendations.
	
The Company has the following Committees of 
the Board:
•	 Audit Committee
•	 Nomination and Remuneration Committee
•	 Stakeholders’ Relationship, Share Transfer and 
Investors’ Grievance Committee
•	 Risk Management Committee
•	 ESG and Corporate Social Responsibility Committee
	
Each Committee functions within its defined terms of 
reference and reports periodically to the Board. The 
Board may assign additional responsibilities to the 
Committees as required.
	
Chairperson
	
The Non-Executive Chairperson provides leadership 
to the Board and ensures the orderly and effective 
conduct of its meetings. The Chairperson facilitates 
balanced deliberations, encourages active 
participation of all Directors, and ensures that key 
strategic, governance, and compliance matters 
receive due consideration by the Board.

c.	
Commodity risks faced by the listed entity during the year and how they have been managed:
	
	
	
Cotton our main raw material being an agricultural commodity poses all related risks. The weather 
patterns, government intervention in cotton producing countries, trade tariff wars between countries 
affect the price movement of cotton. In our Company, we have been following the policy of covering the 
raw material as per customer orders and have graded the buying pattern based on the importance of the 
type of cotton. We have continued adopting the policy of releasing payments before due date in current 
cotton harvest season as well which helped us in expanding our supplier base and thus, faster coverage 
of required volumes. This kept our company maintained in category of one of the most preferred buyers 
in the market and has additional advantage of better negotiation of cotton prices. We have put our efforts 
in strengthening ties with our supply partners so that we are not affected by potential shortages (amid 
Government sourcing of seed cotton at Minimum Support Price during the cotton harvest season) or 
surges in demand for a type of cotton especially in Egyptian, Supima and Organic cottons. Considering 
the likely increased in market selling price, we have taken sufficient coverage of the cotton.
	
	
	
We have also geared up to meet the increasing demand for sustainable cottons such as Better Cotton 
Initiative (BCI)/Organic and other Sustainable cotton. We have continued to source cotton under Physical 
model as well as Mass Balance model. We have been sourcing more than 80% of our total volume as BCI 
cotton in both models together.

I believe that growth must be responsible and transparent, and we remain committed to raising the bar for our

Dipali Goenka- Managing Director & CEO Welspun Living Ltd.
	
Today, as the global dialogue increasingly centers on inclusive and sustainable business practices, we are already 
ahead strengthening our position as a leading Textile company. We are contributing by undergoing a significant 
transformation in sustainable manufacturing, circularity across our value chain defining our commitment towards 
the sustainable business practices. Driven by a strong sense of social responsibility, we actively contribute to 
sustainable development through initiatives in Education, Environment & Health, and Empowerment.
	
In FY 2025-26 we achieved remarkable progress in our sustainability performance, reflecting the strength and 
consistency of our business-led sustainability approach. We were ranked No. 1 in the S&P Global Corporate 
Sustainability Assessment 2025, marking a significant milestone in our sustainability j

ourney. This recognition 
emphasizes our strong commitment to sustainability across environmental, social, and governance dimensions, 
including energy efficiency, water conservation, waste reduction, and employee well-being. For us, sustainability 
goes beyond environmental protection; it is about creating shared value for all stakeholders while building long-
